extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and interpretive guidance for determining when actions constitute retaliation or peer retaliation under the Department of Education's finalized Title IX regulations, and for how recipients must respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation — interference clause
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverse action taken "for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause protects actions taken in furtherance of substantive or procedural rights guaranteed by Title IX and the regulations. The Department treats this as a core element of retaliation and grounds the requirement for a retaliatory motive. Whether an action is for this purpose must be shown by direct or circumstantial evidence (e.g., statements, timing, differential treatment, deviations from policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation — participation clause
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverse action taken because a person "has reported information, made a complaint, testified, assisted, or participated or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing" under the Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause protects reporting, complaining, testifying, assisting, participating, or refusing to participate. The Department declined to add "responded to a complaint" as redundant because "participated or refused to participate in any manner" already covers that activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected persons and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Protected activity includes the exercise of any rights under the final regulations (e.g., procedural rights under §§106.45 and 106.46, a pregnant student's right to a reasonable modification under §106.40(b)(3)(ii), appeals under §106.46(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaliation protection applies to complainants, respondents, witnesses, and others who exercise rights under the regulations. Examples: adverse action taken because someone appealed a determination or requested pregnancy-related time off would constitute retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee participation exception (compelled participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the definition of retaliation precludes a recipient from requiring an employee or other person authorized by the recipient to provide aid, benefit, or service to participate as a witness in, or otherwise assist with, an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department revised the rule to clarify that employees may be required to participate (to avoid conflict with Title VII practices). For employee complainants, an employee may decline to make a complaint without penalty, but the Title IX Coordinator may initiate a complaint and require that employee to testify. This exception does not extend to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student refusal-to-participate protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not retaliate against a student (including an actual or potential complainant, respondent, or witness) for refusing to participate in Title IX grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite this protection, a recipient may still investigate and resolve a complaint per §106.45 and, if applicable, §106.46 even if a student respondent refuses to participate; imposing disciplinary sanctions following adjudication is not itself retaliation if not taken for retaliatory purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer retaliation definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer retaliation applies to retaliation by students against other students and follows the same core requirement that conduct be undertaken for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because the person participated in Title IX grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarified peer retaliation is distinct from sex-based harassment (different elements) though conduct can be both. Examples include teammates vandalizing a locker for complaining or threats to remove someone from a committee for serving as a witness. Recipients must address peer retaliation when conduct reasonably may meet the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of recipient responsibility for peer retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must respond promptly and effectively to peer retaliation when they have information that conduct reasonably may constitute sex discrimination or peer retaliation; they are not required to monitor all student interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are not required to investigate allegations that would not meet the definition of peer retaliation (§106.45(d)(iv)), and the Department does not expect recipients to monitor social media generally. However, when a recipient has information of threats/intimidation to dissuade exercise of Title IX rights, it must take action (supportive measures, investigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse-action standard (material adversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory terms "intimidation, threats, coercion, or discrimination" are interpreted consistent with case law: an adverse action is present when a reasonable person would have found the challenged action materially adverse (i.e., it well might have dissuaded a reasonable person from making or supporting a charge of discrimination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an action is adverse is fact-specific. The Department cited Burlington and other case law; examples that can be adverse include lowering grades, exclusion from programs, adverse hiring/promotional decisions, threats, or disclosure of confidential information. Trivial exclusion/incivility are not per se excluded—the focus is on whether it would dissuade a reasonable person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of confidential or sensitive information as retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate disclosure or threat to disclose confidential information (e.g., LGBTQI+ status, pregnancy or related condition) can constitute an adverse action and therefore retaliation if done to interfere with Title IX rights or because of participation in Title IX procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must protect privacy and confidentiality of personally identifiable information (§§106.44(j), 106.45(b)(5)). Informing another recipient about prior misconduct when a student transfers is not retaliation if there is a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason; recipients are not affirmatively required to disclose such information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiating outside processes may be retaliation depending on motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiation of a disciplinary process or filing a complaint outside the Title IX context (e.g., Title VII) could constitute retaliation if the action was taken for the purpose of interfering with a person's Title IX rights or because they participated in Title IX grievance procedures and there is no legitimate non-retaliatory reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of another proceeding is not per se non-retaliatory; the motivating purpose and presence of legitimate reasons must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality agreements may constitute retaliation when coercive
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a student to enter a confidentiality agreement as a prerequisite to accessing their rights under Title IX (supportive measures, initiating investigation, informal resolution, resolving a complaint, or exercising other rights) could constitute retaliation if done to interfere with Title IX rights or because of participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(5) requires reasonable steps to protect privacy but not to restrict parties' ability to obtain and present evidence, consult with advisors, or otherwise prepare for grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal connection requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish retaliation there must be a causal connection: the adverse action must have been taken "because" an individual engaged in protected activity or for the purpose of interfering with a protected activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaliatory motive can be shown by direct evidence (statements) or circumstantial evidence (changes in treatment after protected activity, timing proximity, differential treatment, deviation from policies). The Department rejected removing this element as it is longstanding and grounded in case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protections and limits on disciplining speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The retaliation and peer-retaliation provisions are not intended to restrict First Amendment rights; mere criticism of a student's decision to participate in Title IX procedures would not alone constitute peer retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should not punish students for protected speech. However, speech that meets the regulatory definition of peer retaliation or sex-based harassment (depending on context and severity/pervasiveness) must be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual/terminology clarifications in final rule (operative language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory text revisions: changed 'receives' to 'has' information about retaliation; added 'reasonably' before 'may constitute' and 'under Title IX or this part'; clarified that recipients may offer informal resolution for retaliation complaints consistent with §106.44(k); added 'both' before '§§106.45 and 106.46' to clarify consolidation requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These textual clarifications align the retaliation provisions with parallel references elsewhere in the regulations and clarify procedural options (informal resolution) and applicability of grievance procedure provisions when consolidating complaints.
